name: Deep Lavender
lede: Deep Lavender is a strong, saturated purple built by pushing plain [[lavender]] darker and more intense, not the pale flower color the name might suggest.

sections.title: Past the flower, into purple
sections.body:
Our library finds Deep Lavender in the 2010 xkcd crowd survey, with no source earlier on file [1]. The ISCC-NBS 1955 dictionary places the same color in its block 210, among the colors it calls "light violet", 5.2 units away in our conversion [2]. In Munsell notation it sits near 3.1P 4.8/12.3, a fairly dark, highly saturated purple [2].

The flower lavender itself gives a pale, greyed violet; "deep" here does the opposite of what a real sprig of lavender looks like, pushing the color darker and far more saturated [2]. Its nearest modifier siblings in the same family are [[dusty-lavender]], a greyed, paler cousin, and [[deep-lilac]], a close but slightly pinker purple [2]. Who coined this exact pairing of words is not recorded in the sources we hold [1][2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: This exact shade does not turn up in any of the 23,781 paintings in our archive within our matching threshold, as photographed [3]. That is itself a finding: a strongly saturated purple like this is rare in paint, next to the greyer, duller purples ground from historical pigments [3]. The comparison is a computed color match against museum photographs, not a search for a specific pigment [3].
